panels.figure_caption: Venous leg ulcers are usually located in the “gaiter” region of the leg as shown in the image above. They can be associated with other signs of venous hypertension such as varicosities, haemosiderin pigmentation, atrophy blanche, and varicose eczema [13, 14].

The histogram of SWE mean values (Figure 4) indicates a right-skewed distribution, characterized by a significant concentration of data in the 10–20 kPa range. This distribution suggests that most lymph nodes examined exhibit low-to-moderate tissue stiffness. A small number of elevated values (>30 kPa) indicate the presence of a subset of lymph nodes with increased stiffness, possibly associated with pathologic changes that we did not account for and were previously unknown to us.

panels.rationale: Real human-patient MolecuLight fluorescence image of a lower-leg/peri-wound lesion in a patient with documented great saphenous venous reflux and chronic venous insufficiency (article: Heinz-Lippman disease as a complication of chronic venous insufficiency). The image visibly shows a wound consistent with a venous leg ulcer, and the caption/in-text tie the peri-wound calcifications to this venous disease, so it depicts a specific clinical manifestation of the configured target disease. Modality is bacterial fluorescence wound imaging, not a standard clinical photograph, hence 'other'. Calcifications (the Heinz-Lippman/calcific complication) and bacterial fluorescence are not in the vocabulary and are listed as proposed findings. The calcific presentation is unusual, so typicality is atypical; skin tone is not assessable from the fluorescence image and ethnicity/age are not stated. [raw subtype: venous leg ulcer]
